title: How MyTeksi Began With One Taxi Company and a Room Without Wi-Fi
dek: Two Harvard classmates designed a safer way to hail a cab in Kuala Lumpur, then started it while both were bound to other jobs.

story.founder: Anthony Tan and Tan Hooi Ling
story.event: Starting the MyTeksi taxi-hailing app in Kuala Lumpur with a single taxi-company pilot
story.summary: Anthony Tan and Tan Hooi Ling, Malaysian classmates at Harvard Business School, were runners-up in a 2011 business plan contest with an app to make Kuala Lumpur taxis safer and easier to hail. With Tan working in his family's business and Tan Hooi Ling bonded to McKinsey, they brought in two salaried co-founders, piloted the app with one taxi company from September 2011 and launched MyTeksi in June 2012 with about 130 cabs. The company, later Grab, had about 25,000 drivers in six countries by mid-2014.
paragraphs: In the first week of June 2012, a small Kuala Lumpur company called MyTeksi launched a phone app that let passengers hail a taxi and see the driver's name, licence plate and estimated fare in advance. About 130 cabs were using it. The chairman of its first partner, the taxi operator Comfort, said passengers were happier.

The idea belonged to Anthony Tan and Tan Hooi Ling, Malaysian classmates at Harvard Business School who had sat next to each other in a class on business at the base of the pyramid. Malaysian taxis had a poor name for safety, especially among women. Working late at McKinsey, Tan Hooi Ling used to text her mother each cab's licence plate while her mother waited up. In 2011 their plan was runner-up in a Harvard business plan contest and won $25,000.

Starting it was harder than planning it. Tan's family expected him to join Tan Chong Motor, the car business his grandfather had founded. His father, he later said, told him, "I don't think it's going to work out, so please don't disturb me about this anymore." His mother became the first individual investor, and he put in what was in his bank account. Tan Hooi Ling owed McKinsey a scholarship bond in the United States, and Tan went into the family business. So they brought in two salaried co-founders, Chew Wei Chuan and Aaron Gill, promised a stake after one year and a larger one after four. The founders invested about RM350,000; a government fund, Cradle, added RM150,000.

They started small. From September 2011 the team piloted the app with Comfort, the only taxi company willing to take the risk, and spent ten months getting bookings to reach drivers in real time. Drivers bought bulk-purchased smartphones through MyTeksi and took two hours of training, lunch included. The first office was a small room without air conditioning or wi-fi.

By mid-2014 the company, by then also called GrabTaxi, had about 25,000 drivers in six countries. Tan, its chief executive, later said he worked up to 20 hours a day, seven days a week, during the expansion; in 2014 he said he had spoken to his father once in three months. Tan Hooi Ling rejoined full-time in 2015.

quote.text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full. If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: MyTeksi's start was a vessel left part-empty: one taxi company, a small room, founders still bound to other work. The years that followed were carried full, at up to 20 hours a day, and Tan himself named part of the cost. Laozi doubts that a point kept that sharp stays sharp for long.

reflection: Neither founder could give MyTeksi everything at the start. One had a bond to work off, the other a family who expected him elsewhere. They did not pretend otherwise. They brought in two others, gave them a real stake, and tested the idea with the one partner willing to try it.

You may be building alongside a job, a family and limited hours, and it can feel like a lesser way to begin. It is a common way. The harder question comes later, when the work starts asking for every hour you have, and it is worth deciding now what you will not give it.
invitation: Write down one thing you will keep protected from your work this month, a meal, a call home or an evening off, and tell one person close to you that you are keeping it.

cross_checks.claim: Anthony Tan and Tan Hooi Ling's plan was runner-up in a Harvard Business School business plan contest in 2011
MyTeksi launched in Kuala Lumpur in June 2012
At the start Tan worked in his family's business and Tan Hooi Ling was bonded to McKinsey, so others ran MyTeksi day to day
Tan's father doubted the idea and Tan put his own savings into it
The idea grew from concern about taxi safety, including Tan Hooi Ling's late-night journeys

research_notes: Early money: Digital News Asia (June 2012) says the original founders invested about RM350,000 and Cradle Fund, a Malaysian government agency, added RM150,000; CNBC (2014) says the launch was funded with capital from the business school and Tan's 'whole bank account'; CNBC Make It (2024) adds that his mother became the first individual investor and the $25,000 prize was seed money. These are compatible, and the story gives all of them; funding is marked 'mixed' (founders' and family money, a prize and a government grant), since venture rounds from Vertex and GGV came later. Founders: DNA (2012) describes 'three Malaysians' at Harvard and a 'founding trio' without naming the third, and calls Chew Wei Chuan and Aaron Gill co-founders; the story names Anthony Tan and Tan Hooi Ling as the originators and Chew and Gill as the co-founders brought in. Contest: DNA says second prize; CNBC (2014) and CNBC Make It say runners-up; Make It gives the $25,000 prize. Tan's day-to-day role at launch: DNA (2012, 2016) says he joined the family business and left MyTeksi with Chew and Gill, while CNBC Make It describes him personally investing and working in the early office; the story says he went into the family business and that the co-founders were brought in, without claiming he did no MyTeksi work. Drivers: about 130 cabs at launch (DNA 2012) and about 25,000 drivers by mid-2014 (CNBC 2014); no conflicting figure for the launch was found. A search summary claimed Tan knocked on taxi windows to sign drivers; no loadable source confirmed it, so it is not used. CNBC Make It (2024) is cited from its NBC New York republication. The office is described as a small room without air conditioning or wi-fi (Make It) and a 'cramped garage' (SCMP via NST); the story uses the Make It wording.
